title: Mathematical Field Notes
section: Count pairs before you count sums
text:
Count pairs before you count sums
Picture a red die and a blue die. A red 2 and a blue 5 is a different outcome from a red 5 and a blue 2. That gives 6×6=366\times6=36 equally likely ordered pairs.
The pairs (1,6)(1,6), (2,5)(2,5), (3,4)(3,4), (4,3)(4,3), (5,2)(5,2), and (6,1)(6,1) all sum to seven. Only (1,1)(1,1) sums to two. So P(sum=7)=6/36=1/6P(\text{sum}=7)=6/36=1/6, and P(sum=2)=1/36P(\text{sum}=2)=1/36.

title: Mathematical Field Notes
text:
Try the experiment in R
Run this code in RStudio or Positron. What fraction of the rolls add to seven? Compare it with 1/61/6.
set.seed(1372)
n <- 10000
red <- sample.int(6, n, replace = TRUE)
blue <- sample.int(6, n, replace = TRUE)
mean(red + blue == 7)
Each comparison produces TRUE or FALSE. R counts those as 1 and 0 when it takes their mean, so the result is the fraction of successes. Change the seed and see how the estimate varies.

Try it
Which total is more likely, six or eight? Find all the pairs for one total, then look for a shortcut for the other.


Show the reasoning

Five pairs make six, starting with (1,5)(1,5) and ending with (5,1)(5,1). Replace each face dd by 7−d7-d. This pairs every roll totaling six with exactly one roll totaling eight, so both probabilities are 5/365/36.

title: Mathematical Field Notes
text:
Follow one point
The shear with parameter kk sends (x,y)(x,y) to (x+ky,y)(x+ky,y). The height stays fixed. A point at height yy moves horizontally by kyky.
Set the slider to k=1k=1. The marked point starts at (0,1)(0,1) and lands at (1,1)(1,1). The fine curves show intermediate shears between zero and the selected value. The point (1,0)(1,0) stays put. Set k=−1k=-1 and watch which way the top of the circle moves.

title: Mathematical Field Notes
section: Read the matrix from the picture
text:
Read the matrix from the picture
Writing the images of the two standard basis vectors as columns gives the shear matrix.
Sk=[1k01],Sk[xy]=[x+kyy].
S_k =
\begin{bmatrix}1 & k \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix},
\qquad
S_k \begin{bmatrix}x\\y\end{bmatrix}
= \begin{bmatrix}x+ky\\y\end{bmatrix}.

The first column, (1,0)(1,0), stays the same for every kk. The second column, (k,1)(k,1), is the marked point in the figure.

title: Mathematical Field Notes
text:
Where did the area go?
Take a horizontal slice through the unit disk. Every point in that slice moves the same distance, so the slice keeps its width. Adding those widths over the same heights gives the same total area. The area factor also appears in the determinant, det⁡(Sk)=1⋅1−k⋅0=1\det(S_k)=1\cdot1-k\cdot0=1.

Try it
Set k=−1k=-1. Where does (2,1)(2,1) land? Which single shear would take it back?


Show the reasoning

At height 11, the point moves one unit left to (1,1)(1,1). Applying a shear with k=1k=1 moves it one unit right again. More generally, S−kS_{-k} undoes SkS_k because the two horizontal shifts cancel.
